title: Episode 9: Top 5 Japanese Animated Science Fiction Things
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DnXALAe3BtY

Science-fiction month continues, and Daniel (@dungeondive) argues that Japanese animation is his favourite medium for the genre outright. Before the list he reads the things he cut — *Cowboy Bebop*, *Ghost in the Shell*, *Macross*, all of *Gundam*, *Bubblegum Crisis*, *Neon Genesis* — which tells you how deliberately the five were chosen.

Fifth is *Akira* (1988), gorgeous and unsurpassed as animation, marked down only because he read the Epic-imprint manga first and thinks the film can't carry the comic's full argument. Fourth, Miyazaki's *Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind* (1984) — ecological SF that, unusually, distils its source manga better than *Akira* does. Third, the OVA series *Giant Robo* (1992-98), seven episodes across six years, "super melodramatic opera with giant robots" where nobody walks and nobody speaks at a normal volume, and where the retro-future style still in use today was popularised.

Then it goes quiet. Second is Oshii's *Patlabor: The Movie* (1989), a philosophical procedural about an operating system, with Kenji Kawai scoring those slow tours through the city. First is *Galaxy Express 999* (1978-81): a boy, a machine-woman, a train, and one self-contained moral SF story per planet. He calls it cozy.

----

Does adapting a manga into a film ever improve it, or is compression always a loss?
